metadata.note: Fast food and counter workers 3.9M, waiters and waitresses 2.27M, restaurant cooks 1.41M and first-line food service supervisors 1.22M (BLS May 2025), roughly 8.8 million workers combined. Covers food safety and temperature control, allergen handling, responsible alcohol service, drive through and counter speed, kitchen communication, food and labour cost, health inspections and the shift lead track.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your food service experience.

key_points: Say the format: quick service, fast casual, full service restaurant, cafe, bar, catering, institutional. The pace and the standards are different in each
Position and stations: front counter, drive through, server, host, bar, line cook, prep, dish, expo. Say which stations you can run alone
Volume in numbers: covers per shift, tickets per hour, average check, team size on a shift
Certifications: food handler card, alcohol service certification, allergen training, first aid. Say whether they are current
Availability last, clearly. Nights, weekends and holidays are the job
strong_answer_signals: Names the stations they can run without supervision
Gives volume, which tells them what pace they are used to
States certifications and availability without being asked
avoid: Being vague about which stations they can actually work
No mention of food safety certification
Hiding a scheduling constraint that will surface in week two

questions.text: Tell me about a time you handled a complaint about food or service.

key_points: Situation: what was wrong. Wrong order, cold food, long wait, an allergen concern, a billing error
Action: apologise for the experience without arguing about the cause, then fix it fast. Speed matters more than explanation here
Say what you were authorised to do: remake, remove from the bill, offer something while they wait, involve the manager
Tell the kitchen or the team so it is corrected rather than repeated
Result: how the table or the customer left, and whether they came back
strong_answer_signals: Fixes it before explaining it
Knows the limit of their own authority
Closes the loop with the kitchen
avoid: Arguing about whether the food was really cold
Blaming the kitchen in front of the guest
A story that ends with the manager solving it while you watched

questions.text: Tell me about the busiest rush you have worked.

key_points: Set it concretely: a lunch rush, a post event surge, a short staffed Saturday, a drive through queue around the building
Action: how you prioritised. Communication with the line, calling out timings, working your station clean, not abandoning your position
Say how you kept quality and safety while moving fast, since that is the real question
Result with a number: tickets served, ticket times held, no complaints, or the queue cleared
strong_answer_signals: Keeps station discipline instead of jumping around
Communicates timings out loud
Protects food safety and quality at speed
avoid: Claiming rushes never stress you
Cutting a safety or hygiene step to go faster
Blaming a colleague for the backlog

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with a difficult teammate.

key_points: Situation: describe the behaviour, not the personality. Not pulling weight, poor handover, cutting corners on cleaning, tension in the moment
Action: talk to them directly and privately first, focused on the shift and the work rather than on them
Escalate to a supervisor when it affects food safety, guests, or keeps repeating
Result: how the shift ran afterwards, and whether the relationship recovered
Kitchens and floors are small teams under pressure. Show you can keep it professional
strong_answer_signals: Speaks to the person before escalating
Describes behaviour rather than character
Escalates when safety is involved
avoid: A story that is mostly complaining
Public confrontation during service
Letting a food safety issue go to avoid conflict

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made a mistake during service.

key_points: Choose something real: a wrong order, a missed allergen check, a dropped tray, a mis rung ticket, forgetting a table
Own it immediately and tell whoever needed to know. In food service a hidden mistake can become a safety issue
Action: what you did to fix it and how you protected the guest experience while doing it
Result and the habit that changed
If it involved an allergen, say plainly why that one can never be hidden
strong_answer_signals: Tells someone immediately
Names the habit that changed
Treats allergen mistakes as a different category
avoid: Saying you have never made one
Serving food you knew was wrong to avoid the wait
Blaming the ticket system

questions.text: Tell me about a time you upsold or improved a guest experience.

key_points: Frame it as improving the meal, not increasing the bill: a starter that fits the wait, a drink pairing, a dessert to share, the combo that saves them money
Read the table: a business lunch on a clock is a different conversation from a celebration
Say what you asked and how you recommended from what they already ordered
Result: the check average, the guest reaction, or the repeat visit
strong_answer_signals: Recommends from what they ordered rather than from a script
Reads the table before suggesting
Mentions check average or a real outcome
avoid: Pushing the most expensive item regardless
Ignoring a table that wants to be left alone
Recommending something you have never tasted

questions.text: Tell me about a time you kept your station clean and organised under pressure.

key_points: Say why it matters: clean as you go is faster, not slower, and it is the difference between a controlled rush and chaos
Action: the routine you keep. Wiping down between tickets, restocking during lulls, sanitiser bucket changes, keeping raw and ready to eat separated
Say what you do when there is genuinely no time, and how you catch up
Result: the shift ran clean, the health inspection passed, the close was quick
strong_answer_signals: Treats clean as you go as a speed tool, not a chore
Keeps raw and ready to eat separation under pressure
Restocks during lulls rather than during the rush
avoid: Leaving the clean down entirely to the close
Cross contaminating to save a step
Blaming the previous shift for the state of the station

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a new team member.

key_points: Say what you actually taught: the station, the ticket system, the timings, the standards, or just where everything is
Action: show, then watch, then let them do it. Telling alone does not work during service
Be honest about the pressure of training during a busy shift and how you handled it
Result: how quickly they got up to speed and whether they stayed
strong_answer_signals: Shows rather than tells
Patient about repeated questions
Connects training to retention
avoid: Leaving a new person to sink or swim
Complaining about having to train people
Teaching shortcuts that break the standards

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you received from a manager or chef.

key_points: Pick real feedback: ticket times, plate presentation, upselling, table attentiveness, cleanliness, tone with the kitchen
Action: what you asked to understand it, and what you practised
Result: the measurable change and how you know it stuck
Kitchens can deliver feedback bluntly. Show you can take the content without taking the tone personally
strong_answer_signals: Separates the content of feedback from the delivery
Practises deliberately rather than intending to improve
Evidence the change lasted
avoid: Reacting to how the feedback was delivered rather than what it said
Feedback that was really a compliment
No evidence of change

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to work a long or double shift.

key_points: Be honest about the reality. Doubles, splits and closing after midnight are normal in this industry
Action: how you managed energy, food, hydration and focus, and how you kept standards in the last hour
Say when you asked for help or flagged that you were at your limit, since that is the responsible answer
Result: the shift covered without quality or safety slipping
strong_answer_signals: Realistic about the physical demand
Protects standards late in the shift
Knows when to say they are at their limit
avoid: Claiming unlimited stamina
A story where standards slipped and nobody noticed
Complaining about the industry hours

questions.text: What do you know about food safety and temperature control?

key_points: Name the danger zone and why it matters: the temperature band where bacteria multiply fastest, and the time limit for food held in it
Cooking, holding, cooling and reheating each have their own targets. Say that cooling is the step most often done wrong
Use a probe thermometer and record temperatures. Sanitise the probe between uses
Cross contamination control: separate boards and utensils, raw below ready to eat in the fridge, hand washing between tasks
Say what you do with food that has been out of temperature. It is discarded, not served, and that is not negotiable
Mention your food handler certification and whether it is current
strong_answer_signals: Knows cooling is the most commonly failed step
Records temperatures rather than eyeballing
Discards out of temperature food without hesitation
avoid: Serving food that has been out of temperature to avoid waste
Not knowing the danger zone at all
Storing raw meat above ready to eat food

questions.text: How do you handle an allergen request?

key_points: Treat it as safety critical, not a preference. Ask whether it is an allergy or a dietary choice, because the handling is different
Know the major allergens and where they hide: sauces, marinades, fryer oil, dressings, thickeners, garnishes, cross contact on shared equipment
Tell the kitchen explicitly and mark the ticket. Never rely on remembering it
Prepare separately: clean surfaces, fresh gloves, separate utensils, and a different fryer where shared oil is a risk
Never guess about an ingredient. Check the specification or ask the chef, every time
Deliver the plate yourself and say what it is, so it is not confused at the table
strong_answer_signals: Asks whether it is an allergy or a preference
Knows shared fryer oil is a cross contact risk
Refuses to guess about an ingredient
avoid: Saying it should be fine without checking
Picking an ingredient off a finished dish
Forgetting to mark the ticket

questions.text: Walk me through your station setup and mise en place.

key_points: Set up before service: everything prepped, portioned, labelled, within reach, and in the same place every shift
Check quantities against the expected covers rather than guessing, and know what takes longest to replace
Label and date everything. First in first out rotation is how you avoid both waste and a safety incident
Keep the station clean and cold as required, with sanitiser and a working thermometer at hand
Restock during lulls, never during a rush
Say what you do when you run low mid service: call it out early rather than at the moment you run out
strong_answer_signals: Calls out low stock early rather than at zero
Labels and dates consistently
Sets up the same way every time so it is muscle memory
avoid: Starting service under prepped and hoping
Undated containers in the fridge
Leaving restocking until the rush

questions.text: How do you take and manage an order accurately?

key_points: Repeat the order back. That single habit removes most ticket errors
Capture the modifiers precisely: cooking temperature, substitutions, allergies, sides, no ice, on the side
Enter it correctly in the system so the kitchen sees what you heard. Verbal additions get lost
Sequence the ticket: know what fires when so the table eats together
Check the plate before it leaves: right dish, right modifiers, right table
Say how you handle a mid service change without confusing the line
strong_answer_signals: Repeats the order back as a routine
Enters modifiers in the system rather than telling the kitchen verbally
Checks the plate before it goes out
avoid: Relying on memory for a large table
Shouting changes at the kitchen without changing the ticket
Sending a plate without checking the modifiers

questions.text: How do you handle payment, tips and the till?

key_points: Accuracy first: confirm the total, apply discounts correctly, and split the bill exactly as the table asked
Handle cash cleanly: state the amount received, keep the note visible until change is given, and never share a till login
Card handling: never take a card out of sight where policy forbids it, and know the contactless and chip procedures
Tips: follow the house rules on pooling and declaring. Say that you declare tips properly, since it is a legal obligation
Voids and refunds go through a supervisor. Unauthorised voids are one of the most common forms of internal theft
Cash up honestly and report a discrepancy rather than balancing it away
strong_answer_signals: Knows voids and refunds require oversight
Declares tips properly
Reports discrepancies rather than adjusting
avoid: Sharing a till login
Voiding a paid ticket and keeping the cash
Guessing at a split bill

questions.text: How do you work a drive through or counter at speed?

key_points: Greet immediately. The clock and the customer experience both start at the acknowledgement
Repeat the order back before totalling, since a correction at the window costs far more time
Work the sequence: take, total, take payment, assemble, verify, hand out. Keep the positions separate when you have the team for it
Verify the bag before it leaves: the drink, the sauces, the straw, the modifiers. A missed item is a return trip and a bad review
Watch the timing boards but never at the cost of accuracy. A wrong order served fast is still a failure
Communicate a wait honestly rather than parking someone with no explanation
strong_answer_signals: Verifies the bag before handing it over
Repeats back before totalling
Refuses to trade accuracy for the timing board
avoid: Hitting the timer by handing out incomplete orders
Parking a customer with no update
Skipping the order repeat to save seconds

questions.text: What do you know about serving alcohol responsibly?

key_points: Know your certification and the local law. Serving is a licensed activity and the liability is personal as well as corporate
Check identification for anyone who could be under the challenge age, every time, and know how to spot a fake
Recognise the signs of intoxication: speech, coordination, behaviour changes, and drinking pace
Refuse service calmly and early. It is far easier to slow someone down than to cut them off late
Offer alternatives: food, water, a soft drink, a taxi. Never let someone drive when you have concerns
Tell a manager and log the refusal per house policy
Never serve someone buying for a minor or an intoxicated person
strong_answer_signals: Knows the liability is personal
Refuses early rather than late
Has a plan for getting the guest home safely
avoid: Serving because the guest is a regular or a big spender
Not knowing the local challenge age
Letting a manager overrule a refusal you are legally responsible for

questions.text: How do you handle cleaning, sanitation and closing checks?

key_points: Know the difference between cleaning and sanitising, and that you must clean before you sanitise
Follow the sanitiser concentration and contact time. Too weak does nothing and too strong is a chemical hazard
Work the checklist rather than from memory, and sign off honestly for what you actually did
Cover the areas inspectors actually check: hand wash stations stocked, fridge temperatures logged, food covered and dated, floor drains, ice machine, under equipment
Chemical safety: correct storage away from food, labelled containers, never mixing products
Leave the kitchen ready for the morning, since a bad close makes a bad open
strong_answer_signals: Knows clean before sanitise and why
Signs the checklist honestly
Names the areas inspectors actually check
avoid: Signing a cleaning checklist for work not done
Mixing chemicals
Storing chemicals near food

questions.text: How do you manage timing and communication with the kitchen?

key_points: Use the standard call outs: ordering, firing, walking in, all day. Clear language prevents most service errors
Understand ticket times per dish so you can sequence a table rather than sending everything at once
Fire courses to the table pace, and tell the kitchen when a table is slow or in a hurry
Communicate problems early: a delay, a missing modifier, an eighty six on an item
Keep it professional both ways. The pass is a pressure point and tone escalates fast
Check the plate at the pass before it goes out. The last check is yours
strong_answer_signals: Uses standard call out language
Manages table pace with the kitchen rather than against it
Communicates an eighty six immediately
avoid: Silently letting a delay run
Arguing at the pass during service
Sending a plate you know is wrong

questions.text: What do you do about waste, portioning and cost control?

key_points: Portion to spec every time. Inconsistent portions cost margin and produce complaints about fairness
Rotate stock and date everything. Most waste is rotation failure rather than over ordering
Record waste honestly. Unrecorded waste hides the problem and looks like theft in the numbers
Prep to the forecast, not to the maximum. Over prepping on a quiet day is a guaranteed loss
Use trim and off cuts where it is safe and appropriate, following the recipe specification
Speak up when you see a recurring waste pattern, since that is where the real money is
strong_answer_signals: Records waste honestly
Knows rotation failure is the main waste source
Preps to forecast rather than to comfort
avoid: Free pouring or eyeballing portions to be generous
Hiding waste to keep the numbers looking good
Prepping the same volume regardless of the day

questions.text: How do you use the point of sale and kitchen display systems?

key_points: Name the systems you have used and be honest about depth. Every group uses something different and they expect training
Say what you can do: open and split tables, modifiers, course firing, discounts, voids, transfers, end of shift reports
On the kitchen side: reading and bumping tickets, understanding the timing display, and what happens when a ticket is bumped by mistake
Say what you do when the system fails at peak: manual tickets, the agreed fallback, and how you reconcile afterwards
Accuracy habits: check the ticket on screen matches what the guest said before sending
strong_answer_signals: Honest about system depth
Has a fallback for a system failure at peak
Knows how to recover a wrongly bumped ticket
avoid: Overstating experience with a system
No plan for a system outage during service
Sending tickets without checking the screen

questions.text: What restaurant numbers do you understand?

key_points: Ticket time and table turn time: how fast the kitchen and the floor move, and where the bottleneck sits
Average check and items per cover, which is where upselling and menu design show up
Food cost percentage and how portioning, waste and price changes move it
Labour cost percentage against sales, and why scheduling to the forecast matters so much
Covers per shift and the day part pattern, since a restaurant lives or dies on peak throughput
Say which one you personally influenced and how
strong_answer_signals: Connects food cost to portioning and waste
Understands labour cost against sales
Names a number they personally moved
avoid: Thinking revenue alone measures a shift
No awareness of food or labour cost percentages
Reciting terms without knowing what moves them

questions.text: A guest says their food made them ill. What do you do?

key_points: Take it seriously immediately and stay calm. Never dismiss it or argue about whether it was your food
Get a manager involved at once. This is not a server level decision
Do not admit liability, and do not accuse the guest. Record the facts: what they ate, when, the symptoms, and their contact details
Preserve any remaining food from that batch rather than throwing it away, since it may be needed
Check whether anything else from the same batch is still in service and pull it if there is any doubt
Report it through the company procedure. In many places a suspected foodborne illness is legally reportable
strong_answer_signals: Escalates to a manager immediately
Preserves the batch rather than discarding it
Records facts without admitting or denying
avoid: Telling the guest it could not have been the food
Throwing away the evidence
Handling it alone without telling a manager

questions.text: An order comes back wrong during the rush. What do you do?

key_points: Apologise for the experience, take the plate, and get the correct one moving before anything else
Tell the kitchen exactly what is wrong so the remake is right the first time
Manage the table: offer something while they wait, and keep the rest of the table from finishing alone
Tell the manager if it is a bill adjustment or if the table is unhappy beyond the plate
Afterwards, find out why so it does not repeat. Ticket error, kitchen error, or a modifier that was never entered
strong_answer_signals: Fires the remake before doing anything else
Manages the rest of the table while one guest waits
Finds the cause afterwards
avoid: Debating whose fault it was during service
Sending it back with no explanation to the kitchen
Leaving one guest without food while the table eats

questions.text: A guest appears intoxicated and orders another drink. What do you do?

key_points: Stop serving alcohol. This is a legal obligation, not a judgement call, and the liability includes you personally
Tell the manager immediately and agree the approach together
Refuse politely, privately, and without lecturing. Offer water, food, and a soft drink
Arrange safe transport and never let them drive. Offer to call a taxi or a friend
Watch for someone else buying for them
Log the refusal per house policy
strong_answer_signals: Stops service without hesitation
Involves the manager and logs it
Takes responsibility for how the guest gets home
avoid: Serving one more to avoid a scene
Letting an intoxicated guest drive
Making the refusal a public humiliation

questions.text: You are short staffed and the restaurant is full. What do you do?

key_points: Tell the manager early so decisions can be made: call in cover, pause seating, extend quoted wait times, or simplify the menu
Set expectations with guests honestly. A quoted wait that is met beats a short quote that is missed
Cover the critical positions first: the pass, the till, and drinks. Everything else can flex
Work the section systematically rather than reacting to whoever waves. A route around the floor beats random movement
Protect the non negotiables: allergen checks, food temperature, hand washing. Those never flex for speed
strong_answer_signals: Quotes honest wait times
Works a systematic route rather than reacting
Names what never flexes for speed
avoid: Seating everyone and hoping
Cutting a food safety step
Letting one loud table absorb the whole section

questions.text: A colleague is not following hygiene rules. What do you do?

key_points: Say something in the moment, quietly and without drama. Most of it is habit rather than defiance
Be specific: gloves, hand washing, hair, a cut not covered, phone use at the station, working while unwell
Escalate to a supervisor if it continues or if it is serious, particularly someone working while sick
Working with vomiting or diarrhoea symptoms is an exclusion issue in most jurisdictions and must be reported, not covered for
Frame it as protecting the guest and the team rather than as telling on someone
strong_answer_signals: Addresses it directly first
Knows illness reporting is not optional
Escalates without hesitation when it is serious
avoid: Ignoring it because it feels awkward
Covering for someone working while sick
Confronting them loudly in front of guests

questions.text: A large group arrives without a reservation. What do you do?

key_points: Check what is actually possible: table availability, kitchen capacity, and staffing on the floor before promising anything
Talk to the kitchen. A large group landing unannounced can stop a service if the line is not warned
Be honest about the wait or the limitations. A shortened menu or a staggered seating is better than a failed service
Get a manager for anything that affects other bookings
If you can take them, plan it: one server, split checks agreed up front, and sequenced firing
strong_answer_signals: Warns the kitchen before accepting
Honest about wait and limitations
Plans the service rather than improvising
avoid: Seating them without telling the kitchen
Promising a wait time you cannot meet
Sacrificing existing bookings

questions.text: You cut yourself or burn yourself during service. What do you do?

key_points: Stop and deal with it. Continuing to handle food with an open wound is a contamination risk
Wash, treat, cover with a blue detectable dressing where used, and put on a glove over it
Report it to the supervisor and record it in the accident book. Every injury gets recorded, however small
Discard any food that was contaminated. This is not negotiable and it is not a waste decision
For anything serious, get proper medical attention rather than pushing through
Afterwards, look at the cause: a blunt knife, a crowded station, a missing glove, a wet floor
strong_answer_signals: Stops rather than pushing through
Records it even when minor
Discards contaminated food without debate
avoid: Carrying on with an uncovered cut
Not reporting a minor injury
Serving food that was contaminated

questions.text: A guest is unhappy and asking for the meal to be free. What do you do?

key_points: Listen fully first. Often the complaint is about being ignored rather than about the food
Fix the actual problem if you still can: a remake, a replacement, a drink while they wait
Know your authority. If a comp is above your level, get the manager rather than promising it
Do not argue about whether the complaint is fair. Focus on what happens now
Feed it back so it is not repeated, and note whether the same issue keeps coming up
strong_answer_signals: Fixes the problem before discussing money
Knows their comp authority
Does not argue about fairness
avoid: Comping automatically to end the conversation
Promising a refund you cannot authorise
Getting defensive about the kitchen

questions.text: An item is eighty sixed in the middle of service. What do you do?

key_points: Tell the floor immediately and make sure everyone hears it, including the host and the bar
Update the point of sale so it cannot be ordered, rather than relying on memory
Approach tables who already ordered it before they wait, and offer a specific alternative rather than an apology alone
Tell the kitchen if you see the same item running low before it hits zero next time
Say why this matters: a guest discovering their dish is unavailable twenty minutes in is a service failure
strong_answer_signals: Updates the system, not just the team
Reaches the affected tables before they wait
Offers a specific alternative
avoid: Relying on the team to remember
Letting an ordered table wait to be told
Blaming the kitchen to the guest

questions.text: Two of you are scheduled but only one section is busy. What do you do?

key_points: Help rather than stand. Run food, clear tables, restock, check on the busy section
Ask the busy colleague what they need instead of guessing, since uncoordinated help creates confusion
Use the lull deliberately: restock, prep, side work, and reset for the next wave
Tell the supervisor if the section split is consistently uneven so the floor plan can change
Say plainly that in this industry the shift is shared, not divided
strong_answer_signals: Asks what is needed rather than guessing
Uses lulls for side work and restock
Raises an uneven split constructively
avoid: Standing around because it is not your section
Taking over a colleague table without asking
Waiting to be told to help

questions.text: How do you run a shift as a supervisor or manager?

key_points: Pre shift brief: covers expected, reservations, specials, eighty sixes, allergen notes, staffing and stations, one focus for the shift
Position people to the trade and change it as the pattern shifts. A fixed floor plan on a moving night loses money
Be visible during peak, at the pass and on the floor, not in the office
Watch the leading indicators live: ticket times, table turns, queue at the door, the pass backing up
Debrief and hand over: what worked, what broke, what the next shift needs to know
strong_answer_signals: Runs a real pre shift brief
Adjusts positions during the shift
Watches ticket times as a live signal
avoid: No brief and no handover
Managing from the office at peak
Doing a station themselves instead of running the shift

questions.text: How do you control food cost and labour cost?

key_points: Know the two big percentages and what actually moves them, since almost all restaurant margin lives here
Food cost levers: portion control, waste recording, ordering to forecast, rotation, recipe adherence, supplier pricing, menu engineering
Labour levers: scheduling to the forecast by day part, sending people home early when trade dies, cross training so fewer people cover more, controlling overtime
Do inventory properly and consistently. Inconsistent counts make every other number meaningless
Protect quality and safety while cutting. Cost control that produces bad food is a slower failure
Give a number: food cost from [X]% to [Y]%, or labour held at [Z]% through a peak season
strong_answer_signals: Names specific levers rather than cutting generally
Understands consistent inventory as the base
Refuses to cut into quality and safety
avoid: Cutting portions to fix food cost
Understaffing peak to hit a labour target
Not knowing the current percentages

questions.text: How do you handle a health inspection?

key_points: Be ready every day rather than preparing for a visit. Continuous readiness is the only approach that survives a surprise inspection
Know what they check: temperature logs, hand washing facilities, storage order, dating and labelling, chemical storage, pest evidence, cleaning records, staff illness policy, certification
During the visit: cooperate fully, accompany the inspector, answer honestly, and fix anything you can on the spot
Never argue or obstruct. Note what is found and ask for clarity on the requirement
Afterwards: correct everything immediately, document the correction, and change the routine so it holds
Run your own internal audits on the same criteria so the real one holds no surprises
strong_answer_signals: Treats readiness as daily rather than event based
Fixes on the spot and documents it
Runs internal audits on the same criteria
avoid: Cleaning frantically when the inspector arrives
Arguing with a finding
Correcting the issue but not the routine

questions.text: How do you hire and keep staff in a high turnover industry?

key_points: Hire for reliability and attitude, and train the skill. Most kitchen and floor skills can be taught, showing up cannot
Onboard properly. A first week with no training and no introduction is the single biggest cause of early leaving
Give predictable schedules published in advance, since unpredictable hours drive people out faster than pay
Respect the basics: breaks that happen, being paid correctly and on time, and a manager who does not shout
Create a path: trainer, shift lead, key stations, certification funding
Deal with the person nobody wants to work with, because good staff leave over them
Give the number: turnover reduced, or average tenure improved
strong_answer_signals: Names schedule predictability and breaks before perks
Fixes onboarding as the retention lever
Deals with the problem staff member
avoid: Accepting turnover as just how the industry is
Relying on pay alone
Tolerating a shouting culture in the kitchen

questions.text: How do you deal with a serious complaint or a bad public review?

key_points: Respond quickly, publicly and without defensiveness. The reply is written for everyone reading it, not just the reviewer
Acknowledge the specific issue rather than posting a template. Templates are visible and make it worse
Take it offline for the detail: an email or a phone number, and an actual conversation
Investigate honestly with the team involved. Sometimes the review is unfair and you still fix the impression it creates
Fix the underlying cause and say what changed, since that is what future readers are looking for
Never argue publicly or share details about the guest
strong_answer_signals: Responds specifically rather than with a template
Investigates rather than assuming the guest is wrong
Fixes the cause and says so
avoid: Arguing with the reviewer in public
Ignoring reviews entirely
Blaming a named staff member publicly

questions.text: How do you keep quality consistent across shifts and staff?

key_points: Write and enforce the specification: recipes, portions, plating, timings. Consistency is a system, not a talent
Train to the spec and check it. A photograph of the correct plate at the station beats any amount of instruction
Taste and check the line during service, and stop what is not right before it leaves
Standardise the handover between shifts so the second shift is not rebuilding from scratch
Use guest feedback and your own line checks as the feedback loop
Hold the standard consistently. One exception during a rush becomes the new normal within a month
strong_answer_signals: Treats consistency as a system with specs
Checks the line during service rather than after
Understands that one exception becomes the standard
avoid: Relying on the team to remember the spec
Allowing standards to drop at peak
Only checking quality when there is a complaint

questions.text: How do you handle scheduling, overtime and no shows?

key_points: Build the schedule from the forecast by day part, then check it against the actual sales curve afterwards
Publish early. Late schedules cause no shows more reliably than anything else
Have a real cover plan: an on call arrangement, a cross trained bench, and a group channel that actually works
Manage overtime deliberately. Regular overtime is usually a staffing gap wearing a disguise
Deal with repeat no shows through the proper process, consistently, since inconsistency destroys the rest of the team
Track the pattern. Repeated absence in one shift or under one supervisor is a signal, not a coincidence
strong_answer_signals: Publishes schedules early as a no show prevention
Treats regular overtime as a staffing gap
Looks for patterns behind absence
avoid: Calling people in with no notice as the standard plan
Applying attendance rules to some people and not others
Blaming the whole team for one persons absence

questions.text: How do you handle a food safety incident or a critical violation?

key_points: Contain first: stop serving the affected product, isolate it, and check what else came from the same batch or preparation
Escalate immediately to the owner or the company, and notify the regulator where required. Late notification is treated far worse than the incident
Preserve evidence: samples, temperature logs, delivery records, cleaning records, staff illness records
Investigate the root cause rather than blaming a person. It is almost always a process, a schedule, or a broken piece of equipment
Correct, retrain, and verify. Then check again a week later to confirm it held
Communicate honestly with anyone affected. Concealment is what turns an incident into a closure
strong_answer_signals: Contains before investigating
Notifies rather than manages it quietly
Looks for the process cause rather than a person to blame
avoid: Handling a suspected outbreak internally without notifying
Discarding the evidence
Blaming a junior member of staff

questions.text: Why do you want to work in food service?

key_points: Give a real reason: the pace, the team, the immediate feedback of a good service, the craft of the food, the fact that the shift ends and you know how it went
Connect it to something you have done, in work or outside it
Say what you want to learn: stations, wine, management, a specific cuisine
Honest practical reasons such as hours or tips are respected when paired with genuine interest
strong_answer_signals: A concrete reason tied to real experience
Names something they want to learn
Honest about practical motivations
avoid: Only mentioning that you need a job
Claiming a passion for hospitality with nothing behind it
Nothing about guests or the team

questions.text: Why this restaurant?

key_points: Show you have been, or at least know the menu, the concept and the price point
Say something specific: a dish, the service style, the reputation, the chef, the sourcing
Connect it to your own experience and what you would be good at here
Mention practical fit honestly, alongside the real reason
strong_answer_signals: Evidence of knowing the menu or having visited
Something specific rather than generic praise
Connects the concept to their own strengths
avoid: An answer that would fit any restaurant
Getting the concept or the cuisine wrong
Only mentioning the staff meal or the tips

questions.text: How do you handle pressure and a fast pace?

key_points: Be concrete rather than claiming you thrive on it. Say what you actually do: work the station clean, communicate timings, stay on your position, breathe
Say how you keep accuracy under pressure, since speed without accuracy is not useful
Mention the recovery: what you do after a hard service so the next one is not worse
Give a real example of a service that went badly and how you kept going
strong_answer_signals: Describes a specific method rather than a temperament claim
Protects accuracy under pressure
Has a recovery habit
avoid: Saying pressure never affects you
No example
Describing a rush where quality collapsed as a success

questions.text: What are your hours and availability?

key_points: Be exact and honest. Nights, weekends, holidays and doubles are the job, and a vague answer now becomes a problem in week two
State any genuine constraint up front: study, childcare, transport, a second job
Say what you can flex on and what you cannot
Show you understand that peak periods are when the business makes its money
strong_answer_signals: Exact rather than vague
States constraints up front
Understands why peak coverage matters
avoid: Saying fully flexible when you are not
Revealing a constraint after being hired
Refusing weekends in a weekend business

questions.text: Where do you want to be in a couple of years?

key_points: Be honest. This industry has genuine paths: shift lead, sous, kitchen manager, general manager, bar management, or a different craft entirely
If you are studying or passing through, say so and say what you will commit to while you are here
Name what you would need to learn for the step you want
Either way, show you intend to be good at this job while you are in it
strong_answer_signals: Honest rather than flattering
Names the step and what it needs
Commits to the current job regardless
avoid: Claiming ambitions you do not have
No thought about it at all
Making clear you are counting the days

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the job is really like:
"How many covers on a typical Friday, and how many people are on?"
"How are schedules set, and how far in advance are they published?"
"How does the tip structure work here?"
"What does training look like in the first two weeks?"
"What is the team like, and how long have most people been here?"
How long people have been there answers more than any other question you can ask in this industry
strong_answer_signals: Asks how long the team has been there
Asks about schedule notice and tip structure
Asks about covers and staffing per shift
avoid: No questions at all
Asking only about the staff meal
Asking something the advert already answered
